# Clinical Phenotypic Characterization and Diagnostic Discrimination of Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 119 (DEE119; OMIM #621304)

## Executive Summary & Clinical Diagnostic Challenge

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 119 (DEE119; OMIM #621304) is a non-coding neurodevelopmental disorder and spliceosomopathy caused by pathogenic variants in the small nuclear RNA (snRNA) gene *RNU2-2* (F1; F2; F3). A fundamental clinical question is whether an affected individual can be reliably distinguished from a cohort of patients presenting with overlapping early-onset epileptic encephalopathies on phenotypic criteria alone (F2).

Based on current multi-cohort evidence, **no single clinical finding uniquely discriminates DEE119 from other severe coding and non-coding developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs)**, such as *RNU4-2*-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ReNU syndrome), *CDKL5* deficiency disorder, or *STXBP1* encephalopathy (F2). The core presentation—consisting of global developmental delay, profound intellectual disability, and early-to-childhood-onset drug-resistant seizures—extensively overlaps with the broader DEE spectrum (F2; F11). However, an ancillary constellation consisting of **episodic central hyperventilation/respiratory dysrhythmia**, **hyperkinetic extrapyramidal movement disorders (chorea, dystonia)**, and **prolonged status epilepticus** provides high diagnostic specificity when evaluating candidates among complex pediatric epilepsy populations (F3; F4). Definitive diagnosis invariably requires molecular genetic confirmation via whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or targeted snRNA pipeline reanalysis, as standard exome sequencing systematically omits non-coding snRNA loci (F1; F2; F9).

---

## Phenotypic Discrimination and Differential Diagnosis

While primary neurodevelopmental delay and seizures are non-specific, specific ancillary neurological and autonomic features provide valuable discriminatory power (F3; F4).

### Clinical Distinction Matrix

| Differential Disorder | Overlapping Clinical Features | Features Favoring Dominant *RNU2-2* (DEE119) | Features Arguing Against *RNU2-2* | Clinician Confidence in Phenotypic Distinction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ***RNU4-2*-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (ReNU Syndrome)** | Severe global developmental delay, profound speech impairment, microcephaly, hypotonia (F2; F4) | **Episodic central hyperventilation** (HP:0002883) and prominent hyperkinetic movement disorders (chorea, dystonia) (F3; F4). Hippocampal sclerosis on MRI (3/5 vs virtually absent in ReNU) (F14). | High-penetrance primary microcephaly (>80%) without prominent episodic hyperventilation; absence of sleep-activated multifocal discharges (F4; F14; F17). | **Moderate-to-High** (Triad of hyperkinesia, respiratory dysrhythmia, and sleep apnea yields >80% specificity against *RNU4-2*) (F4). |
| ***CDKL5* Deficiency Disorder (CDD)** | Early-onset refractory infantile epilepsy, epileptic spasms, hypotonia, severe intellectual disability (F2; F6) | Later median age of seizure onset (median 24 months in dominant DEE119 series) (F6; F11; F12); episodes of central hyperventilation linked to autonomic dysregulation (F3). | Seizure onset in the first 4–6 weeks of life; stereotypic hand wringing/Rett-like hand stereotypies without prominent chorea (F2; F4; F6). | **Moderate** (Phenotypic convergence is significant; molecular confirmation mandatory) (F2). |
| ***STXBP1* Encephalopathy** | Early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, movement disorders (tremor, ataxia, dystonia), severe cognitive delay (F2) | Prominent episodic central hyperventilation (HP:0002883) (F3; F4); prominent sleep-activated multifocal discharges and temporal hippocampal sclerosis (F14). | Early neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy with burst-suppression pattern (Ohtahara syndrome) (F2; F6). | **Low-to-Moderate** (Both feature mixed hyperkinetic movement disorders and refractory epilepsy) (F2). |
| **Generic Unsolved Complex Pediatric DEEs** | Drug-resistant seizures, developmental arrest or regression, multifocal EEG abnormalities (F2; F9) | Triad of hyperkinetic movement disorders (chorea/dystonia), episodic hyperventilation, and recurrent status epilepticus (F3; F4; F14). | Absence of respiratory rhythm disturbances, strictly normal neuroimaging, or mild/isolated learning impairment (F3; F12). | **Moderate** (Yield is ~0.6% in unselected unsolved DEE cohorts [4/672]) (F2; F9). |

### The Discriminatory Triad
A syndromic triad consisting of **severe intellectual disability**, **hyperkinetic movement disorders** (chorea, dystonia, complex hyperkinesia), and **episodic respiratory dysrhythmia** (episodic central hyperventilation and/or obstructive sleep apnea) provides greater than 80% diagnostic specificity in differentiating *RNU2-2*-associated encephalopathy from *RNU4-2*-related disorder (F4). While *RNU4-2* mutations represent one of the most frequent monogenic causes of neurodevelopmental delay, hyperventilation episodes are documented in 60% (3/5) of dominant *RNU2-2* cases (Chiu et al., 2026) and 2/14 undiagnosed movement disorder cases (Krygier et al., 2026), but are distinctly uncommon in *RNU4-2* patients (F3; F4; F10).

---

## Exclusionary and Absent Features Arguing Against DEE119

When evaluating a patient, the presence of certain clinical milestones or findings strongly argues against classical DEE119 (F12):

1. **Uninterrupted, Completely Normal Infant Development and Preserved Cognition**:
   Across discovery series, severe-to-profound intellectual disability is reported in 100% (14/14) of classic encephalopathic individuals (OJ Henry et al., 2026, 10.1002/epi.70473) (F11). Although mild learning disability without seizures has been identified in rare variant carriers (4/16 non-epileptic carriers in E Leit�o et al., 2026), normal cognitive functioning in an individual with early-onset epilepsy argues strongly against DEE119 (F5; F8; F11).
2. **Absence of Developmental Regression Following Prolonged Status Epilepticus**:
   Affected individuals frequently experience developmental plateauing or Frank regression following episodes of status epilepticus (documented in 5/5 dominant cases in Chiu et al., 2026) (F2; F12; F14). A patient with fully preserved milestone acquisition prior to and after recurrent seizures does not match the typical DEE119 course (F12).
3. **Normal Baseline Sleep EEG Architecture**:
   Sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges were present in 80% (4/5) of dominant individuals assessed by Chiu et al. (2026) (F12; F14). An entirely normal wake-and-sleep EEG in a symptomatic toddler with suspected encephalopathy argues against an active *RNU2-2* spliceosomopathy (F12).
4. **High-Penetrance Isolated Congenital Microcephaly as the Sole Cardinal Feature**:
   While microcephaly is frequently presumed in severe genetic encephalopathies, multi-center systematic cohorts demonstrate that microcephaly is present in only 12.5% (2/16) of dominant *RNU2-2* patients (E Leit�o et al., 2026) (F17). A patient presenting with congenital primary microcephaly lacking extrapyramidal movement disorders, status epilepticus, or respiratory disturbances is much more likely to harbor mutations in *RNU4-2* or classical microcephaly genes (F4; F17).

---

## Phenotypic Correlations by Variant Architecture, Position, Age, and Sex

### 1. Variant Inheritance Architecture: Dominant vs. Biallelic Recessive
Pathogenic variants in *RNU2-2* operate under a dual-inheritance paradigm within the same non-coding RNA locus (F1; F5; F13):
- **Dominant *de novo* Variants (DEE119)**: Total approximately 35 documented individuals across discovery cohorts (E Leit�o et al., 2026; D Greene et al., 2025) (F1; F2; F3). Dominant variants typically manifest as classical DEE with prominent status epilepticus (5/5 in Chiu et al.), episodic central hyperventilation (3/5 in Chiu et al.), and hyperkinetic movement disorders (F2; F3; F4).
- **Biallelic Recessive Variants**: More than twice as prevalent as dominant cases, accounting for 91 individuals across 73 families (A Jackson et al., 2026; D Greene et al., 2026; E Leit�o et al., 2026) (F1). Biallelic cases present with profound intellectual disability (14/14), axial hypotonia (11/14, 78.6%), and high rates of status epilepticus (8/14, 57.1%) (OJ Henry et al., 2026) (F7; F16).

### 2. Variant Position and Functional Domains
Dominant pathogenic variants show strict spatial clustering within invariant, ultra-conserved functional bases of the U2 snRNA (F5). Specifically, alterations concentrate within domains responsible for **branchpoint recognition** and **catalytic core interaction** (Chiu et al., 2026; Henry et al., 2026) (F5). Biallelic variants, by contrast, frequently involve conserved 5' stem-loop regions that destabilize the non-coding transcript, causing a >90% reduction in steady-state U2-2 expression (A Jackson et al., 2026; D Greene et al., 2026) (F5; F13).

### 3. Age of Onset
- **Dominant DEE119**: Median age of seizure onset was reported at **24 months** in the detailed clinical cohort of ATG Chiu et al. (2026) (n = 5), indicating childhood rather than early neonatal onset (F6; F11; F12).
- **Biallelic Recessive Cases**: Median age of seizure onset is earlier, reported at **10.5 months** (infancy) with prominent epileptic spasms and tonic seizures resembling Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in OJ Henry et al. (2026) (n = 14), and **1.5 years** (18 months) with 61.8% (21/34) initiating in the first year of life in E Leit�o et al. (2026) (F6).

### 4. Sex Differences
Pathogenic dominant *de novo* mutations and biallelic variants affect males and females without significant divergence in phenotypic severity or penetrance, consistent with autosomal non-coding genomic localization (F5).

---

## Literature Contradictions and Deprioritised Hypotheses

Adversarial evaluation of the literature reveals several contested hypotheses and outright refuted claims that clinicians must navigate:

### 1. The Claim of Absolute Seizure Penetrance (>95%)
- **Contested Hypothesis [F8, F11]**: Initial reports claimed clinical seizures are present in >90–95% of *RNU2-2* cases (D Greene et al., 2025; SE Antonarakis, 2026).
- **Counter-evidence / Reason Deprioritised**: In the large international cohort of 141 individuals, E Leit�o et al. (2026) identified 16 individuals lacking epilepsy (~85% overall penetrance) (F8; F11). Notably, 4 of these 16 non-epileptic individuals carried dominant pathogenic variants, presenting with milder neurodevelopmental delay or learning disabilities (F5; F8). KS Schatz et al. (2026) also documented individuals presenting with "no seizure phenotype" (F8).

### 2. Dominant vs. Recessive: Discrete Syndromes vs. Phenotypic Continuum
- **Contested Hypothesis [F5, F6, F13]**: A Jackson et al. (2026) argued that recessive *RNU2-2* disorder is clinically and mechanistically discrete from dominant DEE119, attributing the former exclusively to transcript instability (>90% loss) and the latter to dominant-negative spliceosomal toxicity (F6; F13).
- **Counter-evidence / Reason Deprioritised**: OJ Henry et al. (2026) demonstrated that biallelic variants also induce direct spliceosomal dysfunction and transcriptome-wide missplicing in patient cells (F13). Furthermore, E Leit�o et al. (2026) showed that dominant and recessive forms share extensive phenotypic overlap (refractory seizures, status epilepticus, severe intellectual disability) and represent a biological **gradient of impact** across non-coding snRNA alterations rather than mutually exclusive binary conditions (F6; F13).

### 3. Hippocampal Sclerosis: Primary Malformation vs. Acquired Injury
- **Contested Hypothesis [F14]**: Hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI was proposed as an intrinsic, primary neurodevelopmental discriminator of dominant *RNU2-2* DEE present in >50% of patients.
- **Counter-evidence / Reason Deprioritised**: Although ATG Chiu et al. (2026) found hippocampal sclerosis in 3/5 patients, larger dominant cohorts (D Greene et al., 2025 [n = 25]; E Leit�o et al., 2026 [n = 35]) did not observe hippocampal sclerosis in >50% (F14). Because all 5 patients in Chiu et al. suffered prolonged status epilepticus, it remains highly probable that hippocampal sclerosis represents an **acquired excitotoxic lesion** secondary to severe seizures rather than a primary spliceosomal dysgenesis (F2; F14).

### 4. Refuted Quantitative Claims in Multi-Center Cohorts
- **Refuted Claim 1 (Hyperventilation Frequency in Leit�o et al.) [F15]**: The claim that episodic central hyperventilation occurred in 35–60% (12–21/35) of the Leit�o et al. dominant cohort was **refuted**; Leit�o et al. did not systematically document or report this frequency. Hyperventilation is empirically verified primarily in the smaller cohorts of ATG Chiu et al. (2026) (3/5) and M Krygier et al. (2026) (2 cases) (F3; F4; F15).
- **Refuted Claim 2 (Status Epilepticus Distinguishing Dominant from Recessive) [F16]**: The claim that status epilepticus (>70%) selectively distinguishes dominant DEE119 from recessive *RNU2-2* cases was **refuted**. OJ Henry et al. (2026) documented status epilepticus in 57.1% (8/14) of biallelic recessive individuals, demonstrating that status epilepticus is a prominent shared feature across both inheritance modes (F16).
- **Refuted Claim 3 (High Microcephaly Penetrance) [F17]**: The claim that microcephaly occurs in ≥75% of dominant DEE119 individuals was **refuted**; Leit�o et al. (2026) reported microcephaly in only 12.5% (2/16) of evaluated dominant patients (F17).

---

## Cross-Cutting Synthesis and Clinical Diagnostic Strategy

### Mechanistic & Clinical Synthesis
1. **Core Phenotypic Convergence**: Generic neurodevelopmental and epileptic phenotypes extensively overlap across non-coding (*RNU2-2*, *RNU4-2*) and coding (*CDKL5*, *STXBP1*) DEEs (F2). Syndromic phenotyping alone cannot reliably diagnose DEE119 without molecular confirmation (F2).
2. **The Discriminative Value of Ancillary Phenotypes**: Secondary extrapyramidal movement disorders (chorea, dystonia) and autonomic respiratory instability (episodic hyperventilation, sleep apnea) carry significantly greater diagnostic specificity than primary seizures or cognitive delay (F3; F4).
3. **Ascertainment Bias in Discovery Series**: Initial index series (Chiu et al., Krygier et al.) systematically overestimated penetrance and uniform severity (F5; F8; F15). Scaled population screening (Leit�o et al.) demonstrates that *RNU2-2* variants span a wider continuum, including milder developmental delay without epilepsy (F5; F8).

### Practical Clinical Diagnostic Roadmap
When evaluating a patient with an undiagnosed developmental and epileptic encephalopathy:
- **Clinical Step 1**: Identify key discriminatory red flags: childhood seizure onset (median 24 months in dominant cases), recurrent status epilepticus, hyperkinetic movements (chorea/dystonia), and episodic central hyperventilation or sleep apnea (F3; F4; F6; F14).
- **Clinical Step 2**: Review prior genomic testing. Standard exome sequencing (WES) regularly misses *RNU2-2* because non-coding snRNA genes lack exonic capture probes (F1; F2; F9).
- **Clinical Step 3**: Order whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or specifically request dedicated non-coding snRNA variant reanalysis pipelines for *RNU2-2* and *RNU4-2* to establish a definitive diagnosis (F1; F2; F9).
